strengths: QuEST addresses a relevant deployment problem through selective finetuning of temporal and attention-related layers, combined with activation-scale optimization. Using synthetic calibration samples and updating under 7% of LDM-4 parameters makes this a potentially useful alternative to full-model finetuning.

The experiments demonstrate meaningful improvements across unconditional, class-conditional, and text-to-image generation. On LSUN-Bedrooms, W4A4 FID improves from EfficientDM's 10.60 to 5.64, while W4A8 achieves 3.26 versus 2.95 for full precision. ImageNet W4A4 sFID also improves from 9.28 to 7.93.

The paper provides useful empirical diagnostics and component ablations. Layer sensitivity and token-corruption experiments motivate the design, while Tables 6–7 support the benefits of temporal alignment, critical-module alignment, and global supervision.

The presentation is generally understandable, relevant datasets and methods are attributed, and a code link is provided. Reported sampling protocols and learning rates support reproducibility. The supplementary discussion appropriately identifies possible effects on watermarking and safety mechanisms.
weaknesses: The central efficiency comparison needs consistent accounting. Table 6 reports 15.25 GPU-hours for QuEST, whereas Table 8 reports 0.45 hours for LDM-4, with different resulting FIDs. The manuscript does not reconcile these settings or distinguish initialization, calibration generation, and finetuning costs sufficiently. Comparable end-to-end costs are needed to establish the claimed advantage over EfficientDM. Actual low-bit inference latency is also unmeasured, leaving deployment acceleration unverified.

The strongest comparative gains rely partly on unexplained baseline failures. Reimplemented EfficientDM fails at W8A8 on both LSUN datasets, and its LSUN-Bedrooms W4A8 FID of 15.15 is substantially worse than its W4A4 result of 10.60. These outcomes require validation of initialization, optimization settings, and quantization coverage. Additionally, the supplementary ImageNet comparison with TFMQ-DM reports only FID, despite the manuscript explicitly questioning that metric for this setting.

The theoretical justification contains substantive problems beyond its acknowledged lack of a guarantee. Equation (11) uses incremental Hessian terms involving epsilon, whereas Equation (10) replaces them with cumulative activation discrepancies without justification. For the output-space MSE used in Equation (12), the second-order Taylor expansion is exact, so large perturbations alone do not invalidate it. Discarding the Hessian contribution is also insufficiently justified. These issues weaken the theoretical claims, although they do not independently invalidate the empirical method.

Evidence for text-to-image quality is limited to CLIP Score and a Q-Diffusion comparison. CLIP Score cannot establish perceptual fidelity or diversity, particularly when W4A4 declines from 31.50 to 28.85. ImageNet likewise exhibits substantial W4A4 degradation in IS, from 364.73 to 202.45, despite improved FID. These tradeoffs warrant clearer qualification and complementary evaluation, rather than treating successful generation as sufficient evidence of preserved quality.

The specific contribution of layer selection and progressive ordering remains incompletely isolated. Table 6 adds trainable components and optimization together; matched-budget alternative layer subsets and joint-versus-progressive optimization would better establish the proposed choices. Important reproduction details—including exact selected layers, quantizer granularity, initialization, batch sizes, and per-stage training schedules—are also insufficiently specified in the manuscript.
